identityReview: Kaïs Saïed, Tunisian president born in Tunis on 22 February 1958 according to the Sapienza-hosted supplied CV, corroborated by indexed TAP biographies. An indexed Xinhua profile instead gives Beni Khiar, which is not adopted over the more specific CV and Tunisian biography. Separate diplomas from doctorate, teacher from unverified tenured professor, constitutional-law association vice-president from a different centre’s president. First sworn president 23 October 2019, second inauguration 21 October 2024. Government and press records confirm current presidency and actual 16 November 2026 meeting.
lifeStatusEvidence: Government portal report published 17 November 2026 records Saied’s completed meeting with Prime Minister Sarra Zaafrani Zenzri at Carthage Palace on Monday. Business News’s accessible opening explicitly dates it 16 November. Both identify him as serving president; the reported service demands and remarks are actual recent activity rather than a planned appearance.

sourceReview.accessMethod: Read the supplied CV’s identity, diploma and career sections; Reuters 2019 result and inauguration reports and July 2021 crisis account; selected DCAF decree/constitution provisions; Carter Center chronology; European Commission memorandum announcement; IDEA October 2024 election review; AP inauguration paragraphs; HRW 2026 report’s selected 2025-event sections; government November 2026 meeting text; accessible Business News opening; Commons portrait rights/history and Quirinale original gallery captions. Scope is specified per source.
corrections: Read the birth, diploma, employment and association sections of the supplied presidential CV hosted by Sapienza’s academic-senate archive. It gives Tunis, 22 February 1958; advanced-studies diploma in public international law 1985; International Academy of Constitutional Law diploma 1986; San Remo humanitarian-law diploma 2001; Sousse teaching 1986–1999 and department leadership 1994–1999; Tunis teaching 1999–2018. Association secretary-general 1990–1995 and vice-president from the 1995 entry are distinct from the separate Tunis constitutional-law-for-democracy centre presidency in 2011. This corrects the raw draft’s association-president claim. Do not invent a doctorate, tenured rank or exact end date for association roles. The CV is supplied biographical material, not independent diploma authentication.

Read Reuters’ short 14 October 2019 report on Euronews: the electoral commission announced 72.71% for Saied after Sunday’s runoff, and Nabil Karoui conceded. The event was 13 October, not the report date or the 14 October result announcement. These were explicitly preliminary results; the public timeline describes an official reported share without falsely labelling this source final certification. No vote-share inference about all registered voters.

Read Reuters’ 23 October 2019 swearing-in report syndicated by Egypt Independent, including actual inauguration, anticorruption promises and the then-existing division between presidential foreign/defence powers and domestic government leadership. This historical division is not the post-2022 constitutional framework. Promises do not establish completed corruption reduction. The article’s 219 parliamentary-seat statement is not used; no claim to have verified the full legislature from this source.

Read relevant Reuters paragraphs on Euronews describing Sunday night 25 July 2021 dismissal of Hichem Mechichi, 30-day parliamentary suspension, constitutional Article 80 justification and opponents’ coup characterization. The 26 July publication date is distinct from the announcement. Dismissal and suspension were later formalized through decrees; the September text references 26 and 29 July instruments. A claim of constitutional authority is not proof of uncontested legality. Suspension is not the March 2022 formal dissolution.

Read selected French provisions of Decree 2021-117 on the DCAF legal database, with Arabic headings and referenced instruments visible. Articles 1–2 maintain suspension and removal of immunity; Article 4 provides decree-laws after cabinet deliberation and includes rights-protection language; Article 7 precludes annulment appeals against decree-laws; Article 8 vests executive power in the president assisted by government. Article 20 retains the preamble, first two chapters and compatible constitutional provisions; Article 21 removes the provisional constitutional-review body. It is inaccurate to say every constitutional provision was abolished that day or that all possible judicial remedies in every field disappeared. No independent constitutional-validity adjudication or exhaustive bilingual comparison is claimed.

Read the Carter Center’s selected institutional timeline and limited introductory passages, not the entire 8291-line report. It separately dates 25 July 2021 suspension, 22 September decree, 30 March 2022 parliamentary dissolution and 25 July 2022 referendum. The chronology corrects the raw draft’s July 2021 dissolution claim. Forecasts, all electoral statistics and unrelated judiciary dates were not imported. This is an observer report, not an official court ruling.

Read the 2022 constitution promulgation preface, Articles 87, 101–102 and 142, and the 17 August signature line on the DCAF database. It distinguishes 25 July referendum, 16 August final electoral decision and 17 August promulgation; no single unsupported precise commencement claim is added where Article 142 links conditions. Presidential appointment and dismissal powers are explicit. The preamble’s celebratory account of July 2021 is the constitutional text’s own political narrative, not a neutral historical verdict. Not every article or original gazette image was reviewed; the database’s duplicated pardon wording at Articles 99–100 is not relied upon.

Read the European Commission’s 16 July 2023 announcement: Saied, von der Leyen, Meloni and Rutte witnessed a memorandum actually signed by Olivér Várhelyi and Mounir Ben Rjiba. Five pillars cover macroeconomic stability, trade/investment, green energy, people-to-people contacts and migration. The June 11 package announcement and July signing are separate. Cooperation promises do not demonstrate full payment, reduced irregular migration or rights-compliant implementation; no unverified funding total or personal signature attributed to Saied.

Read International IDEA’s October 2024 election and turnout sections: 6 October poll, 90.69% announced share and 28.80% turnout, two opponents, Ayachi Zammel imprisoned, three excluded candidates despite an administrative-court reinstatement ruling, and denied observer accreditation. Preserve restricted competition and opposition boycott context. Its 48.98% 2019 comparison refers to the first round, whereas the runoff had about 55%; public text avoids mixing rounds. Official tallies are not a finding that the process was fully fair.

Read AP’s relevant inauguration paragraphs and dated presidency-photo captions. They identify Monday 21 October 2024 swearing-in, amid arrests and restrictions, and report Saied’s justification in anticorruption and state-protection terms. Publication/update on 22 October is not the event date. One body sentence calls it his Oct. 7 re-election; the vote was 6 October and the initial result announcement 7 October, as confirmed by IDEA and indexed TAP. Do not silently propagate the compressed date. AP photos were not visually inspected or licensed for reuse.

Read Human Rights Watch’s World Report 2026 sections headed Events of 2025, political crackdown and civic-space restrictions, including its concerns about proceedings against political opponents, lawyers and activists and inadequate defence opportunities. These are attributed rights-monitoring assessments, not criminal findings against Saied himself. November and December events in this report refer to 2025, not future 2026 dates. No exact prisoner totals or individual sentence lengths are republished as current in November 2026; the full trial judgments and subsequent appeals were not reviewed.

Read the government portal’s 17 November 2026 account of the Monday meeting with Prime Minister Sarra Zaafrani Zenzri at Carthage, and selected paragraphs on prices, fertilizer distribution, transport, health and delayed development projects. Its title records a completed meeting and the independent outlet dates it 16 November. This establishes recent activity/current presidency, not achieved service improvements. Claims about remnants of the old system or intentional obstruction remain attributed to Saied, not independent findings.

Read the accessible opening paragraphs of Business News Tunisia’s 17 November 2026 article, explicitly dating the meeting to Monday 16 November and attributing its details to a presidential communiqué. The page displays a subscriber-only label; no subscription-only content or full-body reading is claimed. It corroborates the event date but is not necessarily a separate eyewitness investigation. Reader comments and allegations were not used.

additionalConsulted.access: Indexed 2024 candidate biography corroborates 22 February 1958 birth in Tunis; opening timed out. No full TAP biography review claimed. The French 2019 biography also timed out.

Search-indexed biography gives Beni Khiar birth and association vice-presidency. Birthplace conflicts with CV/TAP; not adopted. Full body not opened.
Indexed Egyptian State Information Service biography corroborates Tunis and teaching history; opening returned 502. No body review claimed.

Search excerpt describes 2022 power concentration; opening returned 403. Read the DCAF constitutional text instead. Separate LOC search excerpts label the 2021 suspension July 23, conflicting with Reuters and Carter Center’s July 25; do not adopt that date.
Indexed memorandum overview corroborates five pillars; page opening exposed only three lines. Commission announcement is the read primary source, not a claimed full EPRS briefing review.
Read title, 17 November publication and opening sentence stating the president received the prime minister yesterday. Government and Business News records provide date/topic corroboration.
Indexed 9 November Bargou activity report; opening timed out. Not used as full-body life-status evidence or independent proof of alleged sabotage.
Read current crop history and pre-10 September 2024 Quirinale attribution/VRT notice. Private correspondence not inspected.
Read parent-file July 2023 history, dimensions and source; no image pixels inspected.
Redirected to current official gallery and read 24 July 2023 meeting captions, including Mattarella with Saied. No photo pixels or full rights correspondence inspected.

sourceReview.limits: AI editorial and translation review, not certified native-language human review. No original birth or diploma certificates, full constitutional-law adjudication, all election records, complete Carter report, underlying trial judgments, subscription-only article material or portrait pixels were reviewed. Preserve source attribution for government justifications and rights-monitoring criticism; distinguish official tallies from competition conditions and promises from outcomes. Refresh current office and finish portrait visual verification before publication.

translationReview.scope: All 32 display fields reviewed in seven foreign languages against Chinese and English. Preserve Tunis birth and three diplomas without inventing a doctorate; association vice-president versus separate centre president; 2019 runoff, result publication and oath; July 2021 suspension versus March 2022 dissolution; Decree 117 partial constitutional retention and decree-law annulment restriction; July 2022 referendum versus August final result and promulgation; 2023 memorandum witnesses versus actual signatories; 2024 votes versus registered electorate and restricted competition; HRW report year versus 2025 events; November 2026 meeting versus following-day publication. Arabic distinguishes الأمر الرئاسي from legislative مراسيم and keeps attributed allegations separate from established facts.
